raw_text: Mathematics is an essential subject that helps us to understand the world around us and make informed decisions. It is a universal language that is used in various fields such as science, technology, engineering, and finance. Mathematics IX is a crucial stage in a student's mathematical journey, building upon the foundations laid in earlier years. This textbook aims to provide a comprehensive and engaging learning experience for students, helping them to develop a deep understanding of mathematical concepts and skills. The textbook is designed to meet the requirements of the National Curriculum Pakistan 2024 for Mathematics at Grade IX. It covers topics such as algebra, geometry, trigonometry, statistics, and probability. Each chapter includes clear explanations of concepts, worked examples, practice exercises, and assessments, The exercises are designed to be challenging yet achievable, allowing students to apply their knowledge and develop problem-solving skills. The textbook also emphasizes the importance of mathematical communication and reasoning. Students are encouraged to explain their solutions clearly and concisely, using appropriate mathematical language and notation. They are also required to justify their answers using mathematical reasoning and evidence. The textbook includes a variety of resources to support student learning, such as diagrams, graphs, and real-world applications. In addition to mathematical content, the textbook also emphasizes the importance of developing students' mathematical proficiency through fluency, understanding, problem- solving, and reasoning. The textbook provides opportunities for students to apply their mathematical knowledge in real-world contexts. We hope that this textbook will be a valuable resource for students as they continue their mathematical journey. We encourage students to approach mathematics with enthusiasm and curiosity, recognizing that it is a dynamic and exciting subject with many practical applications. With this textbook as a guide, we believe that students will be well-prepared for further studies in mathematics and related fields. Regards, Author

raw_text: Mathematics 6 INTRODUCTION Real numbers are widely used in our daily life. We use them in money and finance to count cash, calculate profit, loss or interest. They help in measurements like length, weight, temperature, distance and time. In science and engineering, real numbers are applied in speed, force and formulas. They are also useful in construction and design for finding area, volume and dimensions of buildings or furniture. In short real numbers help us to count, measure, calculate and compare things in real life. In this unit, we will learn about real numbers its properties of equality and inequality and then law of indices to simplify radical expressions. HISTORY OF NUMBERS FROM SUMERIANS AND ITS DEVELOPMENT TO PRESENT ARABIC SYSTEM Civilizations throughout history have recognized the importance of studying living things, not just for survival but also for practical and scientific purposes. While the study of numbers and mathematics has been a central focus of many civilizations, the systematic study of living things has also played a significant role in their development. Numbers can be represented in language with number words. More universally, individual numbers can be represented by symbols, called numerals; for example, "5" is a numeral that represents the number five. As only a relatively small number of symbols can be memorized, basic numerals are commonly organized in a numeral system, which is an organized way to represent any number. The most common numeral system is the HindwArabic numeral system, which allows for the representation of any non-negative integer using a combination of ten fundamental numeric symbols, called digits. In addition to their use in counting and measuring, numerals are often used for labels (as with telephone numbers), for ordering (as with serial numbers), and for codes (as with ISBNs). Roman Numerals The numeric system represented by Roman numerals originated in ancient Rome (753 BC-476 AD) and remained the usual way of writing numbers throughout Europe well into the Late Middle Ages (generally comprising the 14th and 15th centuries (c. 1301—1500)). Numbers in this system are represented by combinations of letters from the Latin alphabet. From the 14th century on, Roman numerals began to be replaced in most contexts by the more convenient Hindu Arabic numerals; however, this process was gradual, and the use of Roman numerals persists in some minor applications to this day. The numbers | to 10 are usually expressed in Roman numerals as follows: I, 1, MI, IV, V, VI, VI, VII, EX, X. Numbers are formed by combining symbols and adding the values, so II is two (two ones) and XIII is thirteen (a ten and three ones). raw_text: INTRODUCTION Logarithms were introduced in 1614 by John Napier to simplify calculations by turning multiplication into addition. Soon after, Henry Briggs developed common (base- 10) logarithms and published tables that became widely used. For centuries, logarithm tables and the slide rule were essential tools for scientists and engineers. In the 18"" century, mathematicians like Leonhard Euler further developed the natural logarithm and the constant e, connecting logarithms with exponential function. Now-a-days, logarithms are used in real life to make very large or very small numbers easier to handle. For example, scientists use them to measure the strength of earth quakes (Richter Scale), the loudness of sound (describes) and the acidity of substances (pH scale). They are also used in finance to calculate compound interest and population growth, where numbers grow very fast. In simple words, logarithms help us to deal with situations where things increases or decrease rapidly. In this unit, we will learn about to express number in scientific notation and will focus to calculate logarithm and antilogarithm to simplified the complicated multiplication and division problems. We also learn about to apply logarithm in real life situations. SCIENTIFIC NOTATION In the world of science sometimes we deal with numbers which are very large and those which are very small. In Astronomy we deal with large numbers while in some branches of Physics, Chemistry, Biology etc, very small numbers are used. Scientific notation is a way of writing numbers which are too large or too small to be conveniently written in standard decimal notation. Scientific notation has a number of useful properties and is commonly used by scientists, mathematician, health professionals engineers and others. Scientific notation is denoted as ax 10" where 1< a<10 where a is real and n is an integer, which is the standard form of scientific notation. raw_text: Mathematics 6 INTRODUCTION Sets are widely used in real life to organize and classify information. For example, they help in grouping students by subjects, arranging books by categories in a library or sorting products in a supermarket. They are also applied in surveys to analyze people’s preference, in Mathematics to solve problems using Venn diagrams and in daily life to manage tasks like sorting contacts or playlists. In this unit, we will learn about sets, their properties using Venn diagram and analytically. We will also apply sets to real world problems. Pattern, Structure and their Relationship Mathematics as pattern, structure and relationship can be described through examples that high light each aspect.: Pattern Patterns involve predictable sequences or arrangements. For example: In a set of odd numbers {1,3,5,..a pattern exists and we can easily determine the next terms. What will be the next figure in the following pattern? In the Fibonacci sequence {0,1,2,3,...} each number is the sum of the two preceding terms. This pattern appears in nature. (e.g. spirals in shells and leaves) showing how numbers often follow rules that can be identified and extended. Structure Structures organize mathematical objects in a way that reveals their properties. For instance, ageometrical structure like a triangle has properties (three sides, three angles) that defines it. In algebraic structure like groups, clements follow specific operations (c.g., addition, subtraction or multiplication) that allow for predictable transformations. Relationship Relationship shows how different quantities connect or influence each other. For example, in a linear equation like y= 2x+5, there is a direct relationship between x and y as x increases, y changes at twice the rate plus a constant. Relationships like this allow us to model, predict and understand real world interactions. ‘These examples show how mathematics uses patterns, structures and relationships to organize and explain concepts over revealing deeper insights about the world around us. $$ 47

raw_text: INTRODUCTION Algebraic factorization is widely applied in real-life problem solving because it simplifies complex expressions into manageable parts. In construction and engineering, factorization is used to calculate areas and volumes efficiently, such as breaking down quadratic expressions to find dimensions of plots or rooms. In finance and business, it helps in solving profit-loss or cost-revenue problems where quadratic or cubic expressions arise. In physics, factorization is applied to equations of motion, electrical circuits and projectile problems to find unknown values. In this unit, we will deal with the different types of the factoring the polynomials. Factorization If a polynomial p(x) is expressed asp( x) = g(x)h(x), then each of the polynomial g(x) and A(x) is called a factor of p(x). Factors of an algebraic expression are such algebraic expressions, whose product is the given algebraic expression. The process of finding factors of an algebraic expression is called factorization. In order to understand algebraic factorization we consider some types. (a) Factorization of the expression of the type ka + kb + ke In such types of expression there is a number common to all terms of given algebraic expression. ic. ka +b +c). Example 4.1: Factorize 10a + 5b Solution: 10a + 56 =5(2a +5) taking 5 as common Example 4.2: Factorize 6a — 6b + 6c Solution: 6a-—6b+6c=6(a—b+c) taking 6 as common (b) Factorization of expression of the type ac + ad + be + bd For this type of algebraic expressions all terms do not have a common factor. However, certain groups of terms possess a common factor. By taking such factor common, there appears a common factor in all terms. The process of factorization is completed by taking common factors which can be explained as; =ac+ad+be+ bd = a(e+d) + be +d) =(c+d) (a+b) Taking (c + d) as common. Example 4.3: Factorize Axy + 2y? + 4x + 2y Solution: dxy + 2y? + 4x4 2y $$ 75

On the other hand, inequalities are useful when dealing with conditions and limits, such as setting a budget that must not exceed a certain amount, ensuring minimum wages, or checking whether a person qualifies for a loan based on income requirements. raw_text: Mathematics INTRODUCTION Co-ordinate geometry is very useful in real life because it helps us to describe the exact position of objects using numbers. Maps use coordinates to tell us where a place is, GPS system use it to guide us to our destinations, and architects use it to design buildings ona plane. It is also used in computer graphics to draw images and in engineering to design roads, bridges and machines. In simple words, coordinate geometry allows us to locate, measure and design things accurately in the real world. In this unit, we will learn about distance and midpoints between two points and their application in real life along with slope of a straight line with conditions of parallelism and perpendicularity. Co-ordinate Geometry Co-ordinate geometry is a branch of geometry that describes the position of points ona plane using ordered pairs or numbers. A plane is a flat surface that extends endlessly in all directions and it allows us to plot different points on the graph. To locate any point on this plane, coordinate geometry provides a method of identifying its exact position with the help of two numbers. Co-ordinate System A coordinate system uses numbers, called coordinates, to identify the position of a point or object either in two dimension or in space. The most common example is the Cartesian coordinate system, especially in two dimension. Parts of a Cartesian Coordinate System 1, Axes (i) If consists of two number lines; ¢ the horizontal line is known as x-axis. the vertical line is known as y-axis. (ii) These lines intersect each other at point O, known as origin. 2. Origin (i) The origin is the point where the x-axis and y-axis intersect. (ii) Its co-ordinates are (0,0). 3. Co-ordinates of a point (i) Every point on the plane is represented by an ordered pair (x,y). « x-Coordinate (abscissa): Horizontal distance from the y-axis. e y-Coordinate (ordinate): Vertical distance from the x-axis. 4. raw_text: Mathematics 6 INTRODUCTION Mathematical logic is used in real life when decisions are made step-by-step, like in computer programs, solving puzzles or checking if something is true or false before acting. Traffic lights and mobile apps follow rules of logic to work correctly. Polygons appear in real life in shapes like tiles, windows, road signs and buildings. Architectures use polygons to design strong structure, while artists use them in patterns and decorations. Even in nature, honey combs are made of hexagon’s which are polygons. In this unit, we will discuss about mathematical logic along with polygons, their properties and areas and volumes of similar polygons. In the end, we will also discuss about loci and their properties. Mathematical Statement A mathematical statement is a sentence which is either true or false. It may contain words and symbols. For examples: “Square root of 9 is 4” which is false. Another example is 4 < 5 which is true. Mathematical Proof A mathematical proof is the way in which a mathematician demonstrates that a statement is true or false. A proof begins with the information given, then uses deduced facts, and end with a conclusion. There are three main types of proofs. Direct proofs, proofs by contra positive and proofs by induction. Axiom An axiom is a statement that is taken to be true, to serve as a premise or starting point for further reasoning and arguments. The word comes from the Ancient Greek word (axioma) meaning worthy or fit. For example, an axiom could be that a+b=b+a, Va,beR Conjecture A conjecture is a mathematical statement that has not yet been rigorous proved. “A statement that is neither proved or disproved is called conjecture (hypothesis)”. Conjecture arises when one notices a pattern that holds true for many cases. However, just because a pattern holds true for any cases does not mean that the pattern will hold true for all cases. For example, every even number greater than 4 can be written as a sum of two prime numbers. Theorem A theorem is a statement that can be proved to be true based on known and proven facts and these known facts may be of mathematical expressions or operations. $$ 195

raw_text: Mathematics INTRODUCTION Basic statistics and probabilities are used in many real-life situations. Averages help us to find the typical value, such as the average marks of a class, the average monthly expenses of a family or average speed of a car during a trip. Probabilities help us to understand the chance of an event happening, like the predicting the chance of rain, winning a game or the success of a business decision. In simple words, average give us a clear idea of what usually happens while probabilities help us to deal with uncertainity and make better choices in daily life. In this unit, we will learn about frequency distribution, means, median, mode and probability of a single event with relative frequency and expected frequencies. Grouped Data Grouped data is a data that has been organized into groups called classes or intervals. It is used when dealing with large quantities of data to make them easier to analyze and interpret. Construct grouped frequency table For making frequency distribution, following steps are observed. (0) Find the range of the data. The range is the difference between the maximum and the minimum value in a data. (ii) Decide about the number of classes or groups (denoted by k) into which the data are to be grouped. There is no hard and fast rule for number of classes. Generally 5 to 20 classes are considered as ideal. The larger the range the more the number of classes. (iii) Determine the size of class interval (denoted by /) by using the formula. k where x,, is the maximum value and x, is the minimum value in a data. If h=9.1 or 9.8 we may take h=10 for the convenient of size Bclass interval. (iv) Class limits should be written in a way that smallest observation is absorbed in the starting class and the largest observation in the last group. (v) Put the observations in respective classes by listing the entries or by tally bars. (vi) The listed observations or tally bars are counted against each class to get frequency. The total of the frequencies must be equal to the number of observation in a data. (vii) Incase of tally bar method (I!) four bars are placed consecutively and the same is crossad by fifth bar which identifies the five (WN) frequencies in the respective group or class. ee m9

raw_text: Construct a Frequency Polygon A frequency polygon is a graphical representation of a frequency distribution. It is obtained by plotting frequencies against the midpoints of the class intervals and joining the points with straight line segments. Steps to Construct a Frequency Polygon (i) Make sure the data is grouped into class intervals with corresponding frequencies. (ii) For each class interval, calculate the midpoint. (iii) Take midpoints on the x-axis while frequencies on y-axis. (iv) Select an appropriate and uniform scale on both axes. (v) Plot points corresponding to each midpoint and its frequency. (vi) Join the plotted points in order with straight line segments. (vii) To complete the polygon, join the first and the last points to the x-axis at zero frequency. Unit - 11 (Basic Statistics and Probability) Frequency Distribution: The arrangement of data into suitable number of classes, each class containing the observations which lie within the class, is called a frequency distribution. Class limits: The minimum and the maximum values in a class or group are called class limits. Class boundaries: For making class boundaries, take the difference of the lower class limit of second class and upper class limit of the first class then divided by 2. The obtained number subtract from each lower class limit and add in each upper class limit of the data. Midpoint (Class mark) : The sum of lower and upper class limits divided by 2 is called midpoint or class mark. Class interval: Class interval is the difference between the upper class boundary and lower class boundary or it is the difference between two successive lower class limits or upper class limits. Class interval is denoted by h. Cumulative frequency: The total of frequency upto an upper class limit boundary is called the cumulative frequency and is denoted by F . Histogram: Histogram is a graph of the frequency distribution in which class boundaries are taken on x-axis with a suitable width of class and adjacent bars are used to show the frequencies on y -axis. The height of the bars is in proportion to the size of the frequency. Frequency Polygon: Frequency polygon is a graph of the frequency distribution in which the frequencies are plotted against the midpoints of the classes. Midpoint (Class mark) : The sum of lower and upper class limits divided by 2 is called midpoint or class mark. Class interval: Class interval is the difference between the upper class boundary and lower class boundary or it is the difference between two successive lower class limits or upper class limits. Class interval is denoted by h. Cumulative frequency: The total of frequency upto an upper class limit boundary is called the cumulative frequency and is denoted by F . Histogram: Histogram is a graph of the frequency distribution in which class boundaries are taken on x-axis with a suitable width of class and adjacent bars are used to show the frequencies on y -axis. The height of the bars is in proportion to the size of the frequency. Frequency Polygon: Frequency polygon is a graph of the frequency distribution in which the frequencies are plotted against the midpoints of the classes. The plotted points are joined together with a line segment to get the frequency polygon. Arithmetic Mean: Arithmetic mean is defined as the sum of all the observations divided by the number of observations, it is also known as Mean or arithmetic mean and denoted by x. Ce
